commonErrors: Mixing Borden and Cognard type numbers.
name: Borden Classification of Dural Arteriovenous Fistulas

version.label: Borden classification (Borden, Wu & Shucart 1995), types I–III with subtypes a/b
version.detail: Type by venous drainage pattern; subtype a = single-hole fistula, b = multiple-hole fistula.

purpose: Classifies cranial and spinal dural arteriovenous fistulas by venous drainage, the main angiographic feature associated with aggressive behaviour.
intendedPopulation: Patients with dural arteriovenous fistulas characterised by catheter angiography.

options.label: Type I: into a dural sinus or meningeal vein, normal antegrade flow
options.detail: No retrograde flow into subarachnoid (cortical) veins.

options.label: Type II: into a dural sinus or meningeal vein, with retrograde flow into subarachnoid veins
Type III: directly into subarachnoid veins, or an isolated sinus segment

resultStates.label: Type I: no cortical venous drainage
resultStates.summary: Drainage into a sinus or meningeal vein with antegrade flow.
resultStates.detail: Lesions without cortical venous drainage are generally associated with a more benign course; drainage can change over time.

resultStates.label: Type II: cortical venous reflux
resultStates.summary: Sinus drainage with retrograde flow into cortical veins.
resultStates.detail: Cortical venous drainage is associated with a higher risk of haemorrhage and non-haemorrhagic neurological deficit. Management depends on symptoms, location and patient factors.

resultStates.label: Type III: direct cortical venous drainage
resultStates.detail: Cortical venous drainage is associated with a higher risk of haemorrhage and non-haemorrhagic neurological deficit. Management depends on symptoms, location and patient factors.

clinicalContext.text: Classifies dural fistulas by whether they drain into cortical (subarachnoid) veins.
Cortical venous drainage is the key angiographic feature associated with aggressive behaviour.

clinicalInsights.text: Cortical venous drainage present: Cognard classification adds detail on sinus flow and venous ectasia.
Fistulas can progress from one type to another; drainage can change over time.

limitations.text: Requires catheter angiography; CT or MR angiography may not show drainage reliably.

limitations: Does not grade venous ectasia or symptoms.
Three types group together lesions with different behaviour.
whatItDoesNotTellYou: The fistula's location or arterial supply.

guideSections.what: Three types of dural arteriovenous fistula by venous drainage, with subtypes for single- or multiple-hole fistulas.
guideSections.whenToUse: Describing dural fistulas on angiography and communicating the presence of cortical venous drainage.
guideSections.howToPerform: On catheter angiography, identify where the fistula drains and the direction of flow in the draining sinus and cortical veins. Assign the type; add subtype a or b if known.
guideSections.clinicalContext: An angiographic classification; management also depends on symptoms, location and patient factors.

sources.citation: Borden JA, Wu JK, Shucart WA. A proposed classification for spinal and cranial dural arteriovenous fistulous malformations and implications for treatment. J Neurosurg. 1995;82(2):166-179.
